title: China Property Woes Bring Strains to Huafa’s $62 Billion of Debt
reason: 地产困境拖累华发620亿美元债务，中国国企地产信用风险蔓延

paragraphs.text: Zhuhai Huafa Group Co. missed payments on two trust products and is asking to extend loans from at least three banks due to debt struggles.
The company has 413 billion yuan of interest-bearing liabilities and has developed over 200 residential projects across China, playing a crucial role in the local economy.

Huafa's debt struggles have sparked sharp declines in bonds and shares tied to the group, despite expectations of strong local government support due to its status as a major conglomerate owned by Zhuhai.
China’s unprecedented property crisis has just reached another flashpoint, as one of the country’s biggest local-government owned conglomerates struggles with debt payments.

Based in the southern province of Guangdong, Zhuhai Huafa Group Co. missed payments on two trust products that were due recently, people familiar with the matter said on Monday. The firm, which has helped build landmarks such as the 330-meter tall Zhuhai Tower skyscraper, has also been asking to extend loans from at least three banks.
Zhuhai Tower Photographer: Chen Shuoming/VCG/Getty Images

That makes it the largest company heavily reliant on the property sector to try pushing back debt payments since China Vanke Co., once the country’s biggest developer, took similar steps about a year ago.

The development underscores how China’s years-long real estate debt woes are still spreading despite recent signs of stabilization in the housing market. Huafa has developed over 200 residential projects across China. The conglomerate had 413 billion yuan ($61.9 billion) of interest-bearing liabilities, including bank and trust loans as well as bonds, as of March, according to a company document this month.

“Huafa is facing the same challenges as other Chinese developers, but it also plays such a crucial role in the local economy that local governments are highly likely to step in and support it,” said Yao Yu, chief executive officer and founder of credit research firm RatingDog. “The eventual repayment outlook of Huafa’s bonds is not overly pessimistic.”

Still, the news this week sparked sharp declines in bonds and shares tied to the group, which had just priced a 1 billion yuan note in the domestic market at the relatively low cost of 2.07% only a few days ago.
One of Huafa’s offshore yuan-denominated bonds was last indicated down by a record 17% Tuesday, bringing it to about 74% of face value.
Shares of Zhuhai Huafa Properties Co., the real estate arm of Huafa Group, fell as much as 8.9% in Shanghai Tuesday, to the lowest intra-day level in more than a month.

Unlike Vanke, which is only partially backed by a state-owned firm in Shenzhen, Huafa is wholly owned by the Guangdong government, with Zhuhai’s State-Owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission holding about 93.5% and the provincial finance department owning the remainder.

Local rating firm China Lianhe Credit Rating affirmed Huafa’s AAA rating earlier this year, despite its heavy debt burden, weakening profitability and its high reliance on external financing. The credit assessor cited expectations of strong local government support, given Huafa’s status as a major conglomerate owned by Zhuhai.

After a downward spiral for five years, China’s home prices fell at a slower pace last month, fueling hopes that the property market is turning a corner. China’s government recently turned to mortgage subsidies and changes to bank lending policies to step up efforts to support the economy.

Huafa, which derived about half of its revenue from property development and urban operations last year while also running businesses spanning financial services and technology, had blamed the property downturn as the main reason for its profitability swings.
It reported a total loss of 16.9 billion yuan last year and had about 765 billion yuan in total assets as of March.

“Local government-backed Chinese developers are likely to remain under pressure amid weak homebuyer sentiment, falling property sales and limited fiscal capacity at many regional governments,” said Andrew Chan, credit analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence. “Unlike centrally backed SOEs, they face weaker funding access and refinancing support.”
